newsitem.title: USA: Pilot shows Florida jurors smoke stains on jets.
newsitem.headline: Pilot shows Florida jurors smoke stains on jets.

text.p: An airline pilot testifying Thursday in a landmark flight attendants' lawsuit against the tobacco industry showed jurors pictures of large brown stains on passenger jets left by the residue from cigarette smoke.

"Anytime you were close to it you could smell it," pilot Hugh Fulton said as he showed jurors pictures of stained aircraft he had taken in 1984, adding that the stains smelled like "stale tobacco smoke."

Echoing an airline mechanic who testified Wednesday, Fulton said the buildup of the sticky residue within aircraft valve systems would affect cabin pressure and temperature levels until workers used solvents to dissolve the brown goo.
"The mechanics would come up to the airliner with a pump-up spray can ... to dissolve that sticky substance off of the parts so that it would once again move smoothly," he said.
Fulton has been a pilot with United Airlines and Eastern Airlines since 1965. He said he photographed the stains because he was bothered by onboard cigarette smoke.
"There were times on a (Boeing) 727, I almost couldn't see the back of the airplane," he said.
The stains have disappeared since the 1990 ban of smoking on domestic flights, he said. "It's absolutely gone. The skin behind the outflow valves now is whistle-clean," he said.

Fulton was called as a witness for plaintiffs in Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al, a $5 billion class-action lawsuit brought against the tobacco industry on behalf of thousands of flight attendants who say they were sickened by breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S.-based aircraft.
Now in its third week of testimony, the Dade County Circuit Court case is the first class action and the first secondhand smoke lawsuit against major cigarette firms to make it to trial.
Earlier Thursday, the plaintiffs questioned Fred Bookstein, a statistician who is a distinguished research scientist at the University of Michhigan.

He praised a 1993 Environmental Protection Agency report on secondhand smoking that concluded secondhand smoke is a "Class A" carcinogen, causes lung cancer and is responsible for about 3,000 lung cancer deaths among non-smokers each year.
"I quickly recognised that it was one of the best examples I had ever seen of a careful, scientifically correct use of numbers in a public health question," he said of the report.
Bookstein said of tobacco challenges to the data: "I found them to be without merit."

Thursday began as jurors watched the end of a videotaped deposition of Dr. Freddy Homburger, a pathologist who performed years of research funded by the Council for Tobacco Research. On Wednesday, Homburger testified on the tape that the industry pressured him not to publicise data showing that hamsters developed cancer after inhaling tobacco smoke.

The plaintiffs' attorneys, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, want to convince the jury not only that secondhand smoke made flight attendants sick, but also that the tobacco industry committed fraud by deceiving the public about smoking risks.
During the videotaped cross-examination, tobacco attorneys said Homburger had had many chances to publish and asked why he remembered some events in the early 1970s, but not others.
Homburger, 81, answered that his spotty memory was logical. He asked, "Don't you remember when you get hurt in the face... or when someone calls you a bad name?"

The plaintiffs are expected to present witnesses at least through next week. After they rest, attorneys for the tobacco defendants -- Philip Morris Inc., Philip Morris Products Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Lorillard Inc., Lorillard Tobacco Co., Brooke Group Ltd., Liggett Group Inc., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co., the Tobacco Institute and the Council for Tobacco Research -- will present their case.
